claims.text: The initial material is a single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents.
Controlled post-solution aging at 600–700°C for several hours will precipitate nanoscale secondary phases.
The aging treatment will form fine nanoprecipitates throughout the matrix.
The aging-induced nanoprecipitates will be coherent with the matrix.
The precipitates may consist of ordered Ti–Ni intermetallic phases or semi-ordered domains.
Finely dispersed precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion at elevated temperature.
Finely dispersed precipitates will obstruct grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperature.
The proposed precipitation-strengthening mechanism will increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
The proposed precipitation-strengthening mechanism will reduce the elevated-temperature creep rate.
The proposed precipitation-strengthening mechanism will increase creep time-to-failure under constant load.
The relevant comparator is the same alloy in a solution-treated, single-phase state without post-solution aging.
The proposed performance benefit is intended to apply during tensile or creep testing at 600–800°C in an inert atmosphere.
The effect of aging is composition-sensitive within Ti–Ni-based high-entropy alloys.
Restricting aging temperature and time is necessary to control precipitate size and distribution.
The optimal aging temperature and duration for obtaining the desired nanoprecipitate distribution are not established.
The magnitude of the mechanical-property improvement is uncertain pending experimental optimization.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes applying aging to an 'as-cast' alloy and comparing it with an untreated solution-annealed state, whereas the intervention and baseline specify that both groups are solution-treated before only one group is aged. The intended pre-aging state is therefore inconsistent.
